paragraphs: Numerical integration replaces an integral with a weighted combination of function values at selected locations. This paper revisits the Ermakov–Zolotukhin quadrature rule using kernel methods. Its sampling locations follow a determinantal point process, while its weights come from solving a linear system. That construction resembles optimal kernel quadrature, motivating the authors to investigate the mathematical relationship between them.

The central result is a tractable expression for the expected squared worst-case integration error. Here, worst case refers to the largest error over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. The expectation accounts for the randomness of the sampling locations. The formula expresses this error through the eigenvalues of the associated kernel.

Connecting the two quadrature methods makes the analysis useful beyond the original rule. The authors use it to improve existing theoretical guarantees for optimal kernel quadrature with determinantal sampling. The contribution is therefore a sharper mathematical understanding of integration accuracy under this particular function-space and sampling setup.
neurips-2021-an-analysis-of-ermakov-zolo.tldr: A kernel-based analysis of Ermakov–Zolotukhin quadrature yields an explicit expected-error formula and sharper guarantees for related integration methods.

paragraphs: Evaluating generated text requires judging qualities such as fluency, informativeness, and factual accuracy. BARTScore approaches these judgments by treating evaluation itself as a text generation task. Its guiding idea is that better generated text should receive higher scores when a pretrained model converts between that text and a source passage or reference output.

The authors implement this idea with BART, a pretrained encoder–decoder model. Different variants use the generation relationship to assess different aspects of quality. This provides a flexible, unsupervised evaluation framework: the same underlying approach can support several perspectives rather than requiring a wholly separate metric design for each one.

Across evaluations involving 16 datasets and seven quality perspectives, BARTScore outperforms existing leading metrics in 16 of 22 test settings. These results support the usefulness of generation models as evaluators, while leaving room for differences across tasks and criteria. The authors also release an interactive comparison resource to help examine where evaluation metrics have different strengths, weaknesses, and complementary behavior.
neurips-2021-bartscore-evaluating-genera.tldr: BARTScore uses a pretrained text generation model to evaluate generated text across several quality dimensions.

paragraphs: Privacy requirements can differ depending on which parts of a training example are sensitive. This paper studies label differential privacy, where the label needs protection. It starts from randomized response, a classical technique used in differentially private applications, and introduces a version that incorporates prior information, called Randomized Response with Prior.

The proposed algorithm can produce more accurate results while preserving the privacy level of ordinary randomized response. The authors then use it to train neural networks under label differential privacy. They also investigate different ways of obtaining the prior information, finding that these choices can further improve model performance and reduce the accuracy gap relative to non-private training.

The empirical results show substantial improvements over previous private baselines when only labels require protection. A theoretical analysis complements these experiments by establishing that protecting labels alone is easier than protecting both inputs and labels. This distinction is central to interpreting the result: the accuracy advantage addresses a specific privacy requirement, with prior information helping make better use of that setting.
neurips-2021-deep-learning-with-label-di.tldr: Incorporating prior information into randomized response improves private neural-network learning when only training labels need protection.

paragraphs: Image classifiers commonly process every image at a fixed resolution, even though different images may require different amounts of detail for accurate recognition. This paper investigates that source of unnecessary computation. Its starting observation is that, for the same neural network, the smallest resolution sufficient for correct prediction varies across images.

The proposed Dynamic Resolution Network adds a lightweight resolution predictor that is trained jointly with the recognition network. It learns to choose a small resolution that preserves, or can even improve, recognition accuracy for each input. At inference time, the image is resized to the predicted resolution before classification, allowing computation to depend on the particular image.

Experiments across multiple networks and datasets demonstrate substantial computational savings. On ImageNet, DR-ResNet-50 achieves similar performance with about 34% less computation. Another reported operating point improves accuracy by 1.4% while reducing computation by 10%. These findings show that adapting input detail can improve the accuracy–computation tradeoff, complementing approaches that focus on redundancy inside the network architecture.
neurips-2021-dynamic-resolution-network-.tldr: DRNet reduces image-classification computation by learning an appropriate input resolution for each image.

paragraphs: This paper studies collaborative decision-making when clients face different stochastic bandit problems but share underlying global parameters. Each client chooses among K possible actions, with rewards having a linear structure. The challenge is to benefit from collaboration despite differences between clients, while avoiding exchanges of local feature vectors or raw data.

The proposed Fed-PE algorithm uses the geometry of those linear rewards to coordinate learning. A central component is a multi-client G-optimal design, which organizes information collection across clients. The resulting method achieves near-optimal regret for both disjoint and shared parameter cases, with logarithmic communication costs. Regret measures the reward lost through decisions made while learning.

The authors also introduce collinearly-dependent policies and use that concept to derive a tight minimax regret lower bound for the disjoint parameter case. This supplies a theoretical benchmark for assessing achievable performance in that setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the algorithms’ effectiveness, complementing the guarantees about decision quality and communication.
neurips-2021-federated-linear-contextual.tldr: Fed-PE enables heterogeneous bandit clients to collaborate with near-optimal regret and logarithmic communication without sharing raw data or local features.

paragraphs: Attention models use relative positions to understand relationships between nearby elements. On a manifold, however, there is no uniquely preferred local coordinate system for describing a neighborhood. The Gauge Equivariant Transformer addresses this ambiguity by making its computations behave consistently when the orientations of local coordinate systems change.

GET combines positional and content information through multi-head self-attention. Its intermediate features use regular fields of cyclic groups, and the authors introduce a method for transporting these features between local coordinate systems. They also express each point’s position in its local coordinates to separate out the orientation in the surrounding space, achieving rotation invariance.

These design choices allow attention to operate on geometric data while respecting coordinate changes. The model can be implemented efficiently on triangle meshes, and experiments report state-of-the-art performance on two recognition tasks. The contribution links symmetry-aware geometric processing with self-attention: local frame choices are handled within the architecture, while attention can still use both where information lies and what that information contains.
neurips-2021-gauge-equivariant-transform.tldr: GET brings self-attention to geometric surfaces while respecting changes in local coordinate orientation and achieving rotation invariance.

paragraphs: Predicting how several people will move requires accounting for both their relationships and their individual intentions. The same observed history can support multiple plausible futures, so a useful predictor must represent uncertainty over trajectories. GRIN addresses this with a conditional generative model that combines latent representations with graph neural networks.

For each agent, the model encodes two kinds of latent information: one describing relations with other agents and another describing personal intentions. Its decoder is designed to use these codes separately. A graph attention network uses the relational code to learn continuous pairwise relationships, while each agent’s motion depends on its latent intentions and observations of the other agents.

This separation gives the model distinct ways to represent social interaction and individual behavior when generating future motion. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show improvements over previous work on multiple performance metrics. The authors also demonstrate realistic trajectories with multiple possible outcomes, supporting the use of a distribution over futures rather than a single predicted path.
neurips-2021-grin-generative-relation-an.tldr: GRIN models social relationships and individual intentions separately to generate multiple plausible future trajectories for interacting agents.

paragraphs: Stochastic matching concerns pairing vertices when possible connections are uncertain. In the setting studied here, each edge exists independently with a known probability. An algorithm must probe an edge to discover whether it exists and commit to matching it if it does. Vertices may also have patience constraints that limit how many adjacent edges can be probed.

The paper develops ordered contention resolution schemes to improve approximation guarantees under these restrictions. For general graphs with patience constraints, it gives a 0.382-approximation, improving the previous 0.31 guarantee. Without patience constraints, a random-order probing algorithm achieves a 0.432-approximation and also yields an improved guarantee for the Prophet Secretary problem under edge arrivals.

A separate result handles bipartite graphs where vertices on one side have unit patience. There, the approximation guarantee rises from one third to 0.632. These are theoretical performance guarantees for distinct matching settings. Together, they show how better resolution of competing matching opportunities can improve achievable guarantees when uncertainty, irreversible choices, and probing limits interact.
neurips-2021-improved-guarantees-for-off.tldr: New ordered contention resolution schemes improve approximation guarantees for several stochastic matching problems with uncertain edges and probing constraints.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large pretrained model on a small labeled dataset can lead to memorization, especially when some labels are wrong. This paper examines how to constrain adaptation while handling unreliable supervision. Its theoretical starting point is a PAC-Bayes generalization bound that depends on how far each layer moves during fine-tuning and on the resulting model’s stability to noise.

The authors measure these quantities empirically and develop regularized self-labeling from the analysis. Layer-specific regularization restricts parameter movement. Label correction changes suspected mistakes when the model is confident, while label reweighting adjusts the influence of less confident examples. Together, these components address both changes to the pretrained model and the quality of the training signal.

Evaluation covers image and text datasets with multiple pretrained architectures. The method improves baselines by 1.76% on average across seven image-classification tasks and by 0.75% on a few-shot task. Across two noisy-label settings, the average improvement is 3.56%. These findings support combining controlled adaptation with confidence-based treatment of labels.
neurips-2021-improved-regularization-and.tldr: Regularized self-labeling combines layer-specific fine-tuning constraints with label correction and reweighting to improve generalization and noise robustness.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent for new tasks, but its generalization is often largely confined to tasks drawn from the training distribution. This paper targets the harder situation where test tasks come from a different distribution. Its approach expands training with imaginary tasks built from what the agent has learned about environment dynamics.

Latent Dynamics Mixture, or LDM, constructs these tasks by mixing learned latent dynamics. The policy trains on both the original tasks and the generated mixture tasks. This exposes the agent to additional task variation during training, helping it prepare for unfamiliar tasks and reducing overfitting to the original training collection.

The experiments use gridworld navigation and MuJoCo tasks with strictly separated training and test task distributions. LDM achieves significantly higher test returns than standard meta-RL methods in these evaluations. The result supports generated task variation as a way to improve transfer beyond the training distribution, with the reported evidence tied to those evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-improving-generalization-in.tldr: LDM improves meta-RL transfer to different task distributions by training on imaginary tasks formed from mixtures of learned latent dynamics.

paragraphs: Partial label learning gives each training example several candidate labels, only one of which is correct. Many methods assume that the incorrect candidates are selected randomly. This paper instead models their dependence on the example: a wrong label may be included because it describes some aspect of the example’s features.

The method assumes an underlying label distribution whose values express how strongly each label describes an example. Labels with greater descriptive relevance are more likely to appear among the incorrect candidates. The authors recover this distribution through label enhancement and use it to train the predictor, repeating both processes during each training epoch.

To make inference workable, the method approximates the posterior over latent label distributions with a Dirichlet distribution parameterized by an inference model. An evidence lower bound trains that model, and distributions generated from the approximate posterior supervise prediction. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets support the approach’s effectiveness. Its central contribution is to use structured ambiguity in candidate labels as information for learning.
neurips-2021-instance-dependent-partial-.tldr: The method learns latent label distributions to exploit example-dependent ambiguity in partially labeled training data.

paragraphs: Continuous-control reinforcement learning usually represents actions with distributions that cover the full action range. Yet trained agents often favor the extremes. This paper investigates that behavior by replacing Gaussian action distributions with Bernoulli distributions that choose only the two boundaries along each action dimension, producing a bang-bang controller.

The authors connect this behavior to optimal control theory and test it across several reinforcement-learning algorithms. Despite the restricted choices, the resulting controllers achieve state-of-the-art performance on several continuous-control benchmarks. Additional imitation-learning experiments reduce the influence of exploration, helping separate that factor from learning and the properties of the final controller.

The observations also extend to environments intended to capture real-world challenges, and the paper evaluates factors that can reduce bang-bang behavior. The practical distinction is that robotic hardware introduces energy and maintenance considerations that influence controller choice. The findings therefore raise questions about what benchmark success measures: strong scores can coexist with extreme-action behavior whose suitability depends on the costs represented by the task.
neurips-2021-is-bang-bang-control-all-yo.tldr: Policies restricted to extreme actions perform surprisingly well on continuous-control benchmarks, highlighting questions about their relevance to physical control.

paragraphs: Classical learning theory has often struggled to explain the generalization of deep networks. This paper asks whether those tools can still be informative for graph neural networks in a particular setting: transductive node classification. Here, the analysis concerns predicting labels within the graph under study, rather than only the usual supervised-learning formulation.

The authors analyze graph convolutional networks under distributional assumptions involving stochastic block models. VC dimension still yields trivial error bounds in this setting. However, another classical measure, transductive Rademacher complexity, produces bounds that can explain generalization. The result therefore depends on both the complexity measure chosen and the structure assumed for the graph distribution.

The bounds also reveal how graph convolutions and network architecture can contribute to smaller generalization error. This provides insight into circumstances where graph structure helps learning. The paper’s broader message is qualified: classical measures can sufficiently explain performance for some graph-learning problems, making them useful analytical tools within suitable settings rather than a universal account of neural-network generalization.
neurips-2021-learning-theory-can-sometim.tldr: Under stochastic-block-model assumptions, transductive Rademacher complexity can explain aspects of graph convolutional networks’ generalization.

paragraphs: Peer-review scores can be miscalibrated because reviewers use rating scales differently. Selecting the highest average scores can therefore be affected by how reviewers score as well as what they think of the candidates. This paper proposes least square calibration, or LSC, as a flexible framework for selecting top candidates while accounting for different forms of miscalibration.

The framework is designed to incorporate available prior knowledge about reviewer scoring behavior. Earlier approaches often rely only on rankings or assume simple scoring functions. LSC establishes a precise guarantee for one important case: under mild assumptions, it achieves perfect calibration when scoring functions are linear and observations contain no noise.

The authors also report competitive calibration for broader classes of scoring functions with arbitrary noise, extending the method’s scope beyond the setting of the perfect-calibration result. On their synthetic dataset, LSC consistently outperforms selection by average rating. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical guarantee with empirical evidence that calibration can improve candidate selection when reviewer scores are not directly comparable.
neurips-2021-least-square-calibration-fo.tldr: Least square calibration adjusts for reviewer scoring differences, with perfect calibration guaranteed for noiseless linear scoring under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Localization models often predict a probability map and use soft-argmax to turn it into a target position while keeping training differentiable. The paper identifies a weakness in this setup: training through that position leaves the map’s shape unconstrained. As a result, the map does not receive pixel-level supervision through this operation, which can degrade localization performance.

Sampling-argmax changes the training objective to minimize expected localization error under the predicted distribution. This implicitly constrains the map because the objective depends on errors at sampled locations. To make the approach trainable, the authors introduce a continuous version of the output distribution and a differentiable procedure for drawing samples.

The expected error is approximated by averaging the localization errors of those samples. This connects training to the distribution of possible predicted locations, giving the probability map a more informative learning signal. The authors show that sampling-argmax can replace conventional soft-argmax across various localization tasks, with experiments supporting its effectiveness and flexibility.
neurips-2021-localization-with-sampling-.tldr: Sampling-argmax improves localization training by minimizing sampled position errors, implicitly constraining the predicted probability map.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a surface from images requires both a useful geometric representation and a reliable way to fit it. Existing neural surface methods can struggle with thin structures and self-occlusion, while volume-rendered scene representations can be difficult to turn into high-quality surfaces. NeuS combines an explicit mathematical definition of the surface with volume-rendering-based training.

The surface is represented as the zero-level set of a neural signed distance function: the locations where that function equals zero define the reconstructed boundary. The authors identify geometric bias in conventional volume rendering for this task. They develop a new rendering formulation that removes the bias to first order of approximation, supporting more accurate reconstruction without foreground-mask supervision.

Experiments on DTU and BlendedMVS show that NeuS outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods in high-quality surface reconstruction, particularly for complex structures and self-occlusion. The significance lies in aligning the rendering procedure with the surface representation. The first-order bias result is a specific mathematical improvement that helps explain the reported reconstruction gains.
neurips-2021-neus-learning-neural-implic.tldr: NeuS combines a neural signed distance surface with rendering that removes first-order geometric bias to improve reconstruction from images.

paragraphs: This paper studies markets where items arrive sequentially and must receive prices and allocations that cannot later be revised. Buyers initially have linear, additive utilities. The authors define an online market equilibrium through sequences of prices and allocations that satisfy buyer optimality and market clearance when considered in hindsight.

Their allocation and pricing dynamics, PACE, have asymptotic guarantees when items are drawn independently from the same unknown distribution. Buyers’ average utilities converge to those of a corresponding static market, and their average spending converges to their per-period budgets. The unknown distribution may have continuous support, so the analysis accommodates that form of item variation.

These convergence results also deliver familiar fair-division properties asymptotically, including envy-freeness, Pareto optimality, and proportional shares. The authors extend the dynamics to quasilinear utilities, obtaining an online algorithm for first-price pacing equilibria. Experiments on real and synthetic data show fast convergence under several metrics. The fairness conclusions concern long-run behavior under the stated arrival assumption, rather than guarantees for every individual allocation.
neurips-2021-online-market-equilibrium-w.tldr: PACE allocates and prices arriving items with asymptotic equilibrium and fairness guarantees under independent, identically distributed arrivals.

paragraphs: Interpretability techniques can identify image regions that matter for a neural network’s decisions. This paper asks whether those regions also matter to people. Using 79 experiments with 7,810 participants, the authors compare passive attention maps from artificial neural networks with human visual selectivity measured through six behavioral tasks, including recognition, localization, viewing, and search.

The comparisons reveal significant overlap between network attention and human selectivity. Among the evaluated approaches, guided-backpropagation visualizations from relatively simple architectures best predict a component shared across the human measures. This focuses the comparison on common variation across behaviors, rather than treating any single task as a complete description of human vision.

Recognition experiments also manipulate which image information remains visible. People classify images more easily under masks derived from network attention than under control masks. Conversely, masks based on human selectivity affect recognition in the same networks. These interventions complement the correlations and support visual selectivity as a way to assess how artificial networks resemble, and differ from, human vision.
neurips-2021-passive-attention-in-artifi.tldr: Neural-network attention maps overlap with human visual selectivity, and masking experiments show that the selected regions influence recognition.

paragraphs: A ReLU network can sometimes be compressed without changing its function over a specified input domain. The opportunity comes from stable neurons, whose activation status does not change within that domain. Identifying them has been costly because previous approaches require solving, or adequately approximating, multiple discrete optimization problems.

This paper introduces an algorithm that identifies all stable neurons through a single optimization problem. On CIFAR-10, its median speedup over the state-of-the-art method is 183 times. That improvement makes it possible to investigate exact compression of deeper networks with five layers of 100 neurons and wider networks with two layers of 800 neurons within minutes.

For classifiers trained with an amount of L1 regularization that does not reduce accuracy, the authors remove up to 56% of connections on CIFAR-10. The exactness claim is tied to the specified input domain: within it, the compressed network preserves the original functionality. The contribution makes the search for such removable structure substantially more practical.
neurips-2021-scaling-up-exact-neural-net.tldr: A single optimization problem identifies stable ReLU neurons much faster, enabling compression that exactly preserves network behavior on a specified input domain.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models define their computations through implicit relationships, which makes standard certification tools for conventional networks difficult to apply directly. This paper focuses on monotone operator equilibrium networks, or monDEQs, with ReLU activations. It develops a mathematical representation that makes several certification questions accessible through semidefinite programming.

The representation is semialgebraic, expressing the network through polynomial relationships and inequalities. From it, the authors construct semidefinite-program approximations to the input–output relation. They apply these models to robustness certification, estimation of Lipschitz constants, and propagation of ellipsoidal uncertainty. These tasks examine how output behavior can be bounded as inputs vary.

The resulting models certify robustness with respect to general Lp norms and outperform existing monDEQ certification approaches in the reported experiments. The investigations also suggest greater robustness to L2 perturbations than to L-infinity perturbations. That comparison is presented as an experimental indication. The broader contribution is a shared optimization-based framework for examining several kinds of guarantees in an implicitly defined network.
neurips-2021-semialgebraic-representatio.tldr: A semialgebraic representation enables semidefinite-program certification of robustness and related properties for ReLU-based monotone equilibrium networks.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to adapt to a new task using only a small amount of labeled data. Pretraining features has become an important part of successful approaches, but its connection to meta-learning has lacked theoretical explanation. This paper investigates that connection, emphasizing the role of global labels shared across tasks.

The authors show theoretically why pretraining can benefit meta-learning and why shared label information matters to that benefit. This also exposes a practical obstacle: global labels may be unavailable even when individual training tasks have their own labels. The proposed Meta Label Learning framework, MeLa, addresses this by automatically inferring global labels.

MeLa uses this inferred information to obtain robust few-shot models. Empirical evaluations find it competitive with existing methods, and ablation experiments examine its key properties. The contribution joins an explanation of pretraining’s value with a method aimed at supplying the shared label structure that pretraining needs, extending the approach to situations where that structure is not directly provided.
neurips-2021-the-role-of-global-labels-i.tldr: MeLa infers labels shared across tasks, motivated by a theoretical account of why global labels make pretraining useful for few-shot learning.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can suffer from over-smoothing and sensitivity to changes in graph structure. This paper introduces topological relational inference, or TRI, to incorporate higher-order structural information into their learning. The approach examines small neighborhoods around nodes, giving the model additional information about local organization beyond the original graph connections.

TRI uses persistent homology to summarize these neighborhoods and then rewires the graph using the resulting topological information. It also supplies the summaries as side information to the local learning algorithm. This combines conventional graph structure with higher-order properties. The authors derive stability properties for the local topological representation and discuss implications for the graph’s algebraic connectivity.

On node-classification tasks, TRI-GNN outperforms all 14 compared state-of-the-art baselines on six of seven graphs. It also shows greater robustness to perturbations, with improvements of up to 10% in noisy scenarios. These findings support topology-informed rewiring and auxiliary information as useful ways to improve graph learning, with the reported gains varying across the evaluated graphs and conditions.
neurips-2021-topological-relational-lear.tldr: TRI uses local topological summaries to rewire graphs and enrich graph neural networks, improving node classification and robustness in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Lookahead maintains fast weights updated repeatedly by an inner optimizer and slow weights updated using the latest fast weights. Although it often improves test performance, the reason has lacked theoretical explanation. This paper analyzes that advantage through excess risk, connecting performance to the balance between optimization error and generalization error.

The authors prove that Lookahead with SGD can achieve a better balance and smaller excess risk than ordinary SGD for convex and strongly convex problems, and for nonconvex problems satisfying the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. They also show that stagewise learning-rate reductions can improve Lookahead’s optimization and generalization behavior on strongly convex problems.

Building on this analysis, the paper proposes stagewise locally-regularized Lookahead, or SLRLA. Each stage optimizes the original objective together with a local regularizer, and the authors establish improvements over conventional stagewise Lookahead in their theoretical analysis. Experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet support its advantages. The theoretical explanation rests on specified problem conditions, while the image experiments provide complementary empirical evidence.
neurips-2021-towards-understanding-why-l.tldr: The paper explains Lookahead’s advantages under specified optimization conditions and develops a stagewise, locally regularized variant with further improvements.

paragraphs: Conditional image generation may need to follow text, reference images, selected image regions that must be preserved, or combinations of these instructions. UFC-BERT brings these controls into one two-stage architecture. It represents both the guidance and the image being generated as sequences of discrete tokens that a Transformer can process.

The second stage uses non-autoregressive generation, avoiding the sequential generation strategy used by the compared autoregressive approaches. This choice is intended to improve overall image consistency, support preservation of specified image blocks, and increase synthesis speed. A progressive algorithm then repeatedly refines the generated image using two estimators: one for adherence to the controls and one for image fidelity.

Experiments on M2C-Fashion and Multi-Modal CelebA-HQ show that the method can produce high-fidelity images while following flexible combinations of controls. The contribution is the combination of a common representation for different instructions with a refinement process that evaluates both compliance and visual quality. This lets several forms of guidance participate in the same synthesis framework.
neurips-2021-ufc-bert-unifying-multi-mod.tldr: UFC-BERT unifies text, image references, and preserved image regions as token-based controls for progressively refined image generation.

paragraphs: Predicting a changing scene becomes difficult when objects disappear from view and later return. This paper develops an object-based transition model that separates a scene into object slots and predicts how those objects evolve across frames. A central challenge is keeping each slot associated with the same object over time.

The model introduces an alignment module that matches objects to a slot-wise memory, maintaining consistent ordering across observations. Training is end-to-end and unsupervised. Its transition losses operate on the structured object representation rather than on pixels, connecting the prediction objective to the objects whose evolution the model is intended to track.

The authors show that combining object-level losses with correct temporal alignment outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline. The model also handles occlusion and reappearance well in partially observable environments. These findings emphasize the importance of both persistence and identity: useful prediction requires maintaining an object’s representation through changes in visibility and preserving which object that representation refers to across time.
neurips-2021-unsupervised-object-based-t.tldr: An unsupervised object-transition model uses memory-based alignment and object-level losses to track identity through occlusion and predict scene changes.
